author: Kyle St. Clair
title: Historical marker to honor Florence school, foster home that served Black children - NewsBreak
text:
By Kyle St. Clair ,
59 minutes ago
FLORENCE, S.C. (WBTW) — The City of Florence announced a new historical marker will be dedicated later this month in Florence to recognize a property that served generations of Black children through education and community programs.
The marker, recognizing the history of the Palmetto School and Florence County Foster Home for Negro Children, will be dedicated at 6 p.m. Sept. 15 at 1511 Stokes Road, according to a joint news release from the City of Florence and Francis Marion University.
The Palmetto School opened around 1920 as a rural school for Black children in Florence School District 1, according to the release. The wooden schoolhouse sat on two acres and was rebuilt using Works Progress Administration materials following a fire in 1941.
By 1945, the school served more than 60 students and included a cafeteria and piano for music classes.
After the school closed following a reorganization of the school district, the building became the Florence County Foster Home for Colored Children, as it was then known, in October 1953. Under the leadership of Dr. Iola Jones, the Florence Council of Negro Women helped establish the home, securing a 20-year lease and raising money with support from Florence County and the surrounding community.
Women including Lubertha Myers worked to provide opportunities for children through community support, including teaching them to garden and connecting them with people who could teach them trades, according to the release.
The Florence Council of Negro Women purchased the property in 1967 for $2,002. The foster home closed in 1969 after serving more than 300 Black children.
The property continued to serve the community, reopening in 1978 as the Bethune-Jones Career Center and School of Cosmetology. In 1994, the Pee Dee Community Action Agency acquired the property and opened the Bethune Jones Child Development Center, which operated as a Head Start center.
The historical marker was prepared by Universities Studying Slavery at Francis Marion University. The release said the marker is intended to recognize the property’s history and the leadership of Black women who worked to serve their community.
The Sept. 15 dedication program is scheduled to include remarks from Florence County Council Chairman Jerry W. Yarborough Jr.; Florence 1 Schools board member EJ McIver; Florence Section of the National Council of Negro Women President Modestine Samuel; Florence Mayor Lethonia Barnes; FMU African and African American Studies Co-director Dr. Erica Johnson; and Florence City Manager Scotty Davis.
